subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Attention Networks
description: A quick win: understand The Attention Networks.

hook.text: Michael Posner mapped three separate attention networks in the brain, each with its own wiring.

buildup.text: The alerting network uses norepinephrine to maintain readiness. It keeps you awake and prepared.

discovery.text: The orienting network, driven by the parietal cortex, shifts focus to relevant locations in space.

twist.text: The executive network, centered in the prefrontal cortex, resolves conflicts between competing signals.

climax.text: Posner's Attention Network Test can measure each system independently in a single 20-minute session.

punchline.text: Three networks, three chemicals, three jobs.

quiz.question: Which network resolves conflicts between competing signals?

details.summary: Michael Posner identified three distinct attention networks in the brain: alerting, which maintains readiness; orienting, which selects sensory input; and executive control, which resolves conflicts. Each network has its own neural circuitry and neurotransmitter system.
details.whyItMatters: Posner's three-network model transformed attention from a single concept into a measurable set of distinct functions, enabling targeted research on disorders like ADHD.
takeaways: Three networks: alerting, orienting, and executive control
Each has distinct brain regions and neurotransmitter systems
The Attention Network Test measures all three independently

faq.question: How are the three attention networks measured?
faq.answer: Posner's Attention Network Test presents flanker tasks with cues. Alerting is measured by comparing cued versus uncued trials. Orienting is measured by comparing valid versus invalid spatial cues. Executive control is measured by interference from conflicting flankers.

faq.question: Which neurotransmitters control each network?
faq.answer: The alerting network relies heavily on norepinephrine. The orienting network depends on acetylcholine. The executive control network is modulated by dopamine. This specificity explains why different drugs affect different aspects of attention.
